method: Flesch Kincaid grade plus five, using a vowel-group syllable heuristic. Punctuated sentences and standalone task lines are counted as sentence units. Exact corpora and hashes retained. Quantity table fragments, headings, staff text, dates, lesson codes and the verbatim scheme outcome are excluded. Estimates guide editing; they are not learner assessments. Read-aloud and confirmed scribing routes are available.

Use the actual item and agreed method. The adult checks and supervises tools. Finish only what can be done safely in the lesson.
Put tools down and compare the actual item with the design. The adult checks that the fabric, thread and any bonding route are suitable. Count and control all needles before work.
With the agreed support, secure loose thread ends. For a hand-stitch end, take a small stitch through both layers on the back. Leave a loop before pulling tight. Pass the needle through the loop and pull snug. Repeat once. Trim only the loose tail with agreed scissors. Do not cut the seam or fabric.
Return and count all needles and other tools. Check that no sharp parts remain in the item. Test only when it is safe. If adhesive was used, wait for its full labelled cure before testing.
If the actual approved design used bonding, follow its real label and adult instructions. No cure time is invented. Keep strength and handling tests pending until the full labelled cure is complete.
Put tools down if a needle is unaccounted for, the method changes or you need more help. For a missing or broken needle, stop and keep the area clear. The adult recovers and accounts for all parts and controls disposal. Do not release or test the pouch until all sharp parts are accounted for. Return every tool to the agreed container.
I finished ___. I did ___. The adult did ___. A check still pending is ___.
No actual item or safe tools: use a model or oral sequence and label it simulation. Actual textile finishing stays pending.

The adult clears the actual item before any test. Remove and count all needles. Wait for full labelled adhesive cure if bonding was used.
Place the actual three 60 mm by 80 mm paper cards into the pouch without forcing them.
Do all three fit? What did you see?
Hold the pouch upright and lift it gently over the table. Do not shake it or turn it upside down.
Do the joined sides and bottom hold during this gentle check?
Look at edges and joins. Check handling only after the adult clears the item.
Are loose threads secured and sharp parts removed? Is it comfortable to handle?
In your book: test ___. What I actually did ___. What happened ___. What this shows about the purpose ___. Help used ___. If not tested, why it is pending ___.
Use the same three cards for the fit and upright check. Do not force them in, shake the item or turn it upside down. A gentle classroom check gives limited evidence, not a guarantee of long-term durability.
Say what you predict, and label it a prediction or simulation. Do not write a result as though the test happened.

Use this invented brief with your actual Week 4 design and Week 5 work. Any approved change must be recorded; the class model is not a pupil result.
A small reusable pouch for three paper prompt cards, each 60 mm by 80 mm. The top stays open. It should hold the cards upright, have joined sides and bottom, contain no loose sharp parts and be comfortable to handle.
Default model: two fabric pieces, each 100 mm wide by 120 mm high. A seam line is 10 mm inside the left, right and bottom edges. Leave the top open. Default join is hand running stitch. Use each pupil’s actual approved design and any recorded change.
Do three actual cards fit without force? Do joined edges hold during a gentle upright lift over the table? Are loose ends secure, sharp parts removed and handling comfortable?
In your book: my actual fabric and join ___. A real approved change ___. Where my design is kept ___. What remains unfinished ___.
A drawing or prediction does not prove the item was made or tested. Keep gaps and support visible.

An adult model is not your evaluation. Unfinished work and an honest failed test can give useful evidence for your next step.

Weekly outcome verbatim: TEXTILES: finish and evaluate a textile product.
This is the assessing week.
I can finish my item safely, test its purpose and explain what the evidence shows.
[ ] I can complete or direct an agreed finishing action and record the help used.
[ ] I can test the pouch against its purpose and give my own evidence-based view.
[ ] I can check the six weekly outcomes honestly and choose a next step.
Secure the agreed loose ends, trim only approved loose tails, count and return tools, and check for sharp parts. Test only when the actual item is cleared and any adhesive has fully cured.
A small reusable pouch for three paper prompt cards, each 60 mm by 80 mm. The top stays open. It should hold the cards upright, have joined sides and bottom, contain no loose sharp parts and be comfortable to handle.
A prediction says what may happen. A test result records what actually happened. My evaluation uses that result to explain what worked and one useful improvement.
Use the Evidence Sheet grid with real work. Choose Shown, More to do or Not yet seen and add a date, location and comment. A tick is weekly evidence, not an award decision.
In your book. Rehearse in any language. Point, speak, sign or direct an adult where needed. Keep actual help and unfinished work visible.
